key_facts: Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang days after rejecting his offer to return, less than two weeks after he resigned on 12 November over reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. Trump said he 'made the deal' and 'convinced' the board; the board said it received input from senior US government levels and was confident the reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Nvidia stock jumped 31% after Huang's reappointment on Monday, adding about $1tn to market value, though the closing price was still slightly below the Friday morning opening price. Huang's return helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO. Huang is scheduled for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December and has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee two days later.

A BBC review of Trump's government financial disclosures shows he bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m across 85 purchases, and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m from 19 sales. Democrats accused the administration of selling out national security for financial gain; Trump and the White House have rejected claims he profited from the presidency.
importance_reason: Reinstatement of the CEO of the world's most valuable chipmaker after a ~$1tn market swing, with White House involvement, congressional investigations and a presidential stake in the stock.
market_link: Nvidia is a major driver of US equity indices and AI-linked valuations; its share price swing moved the S&P 500 out of correction territory, and export-control enforcement affects chip-sector outlook.

key_facts: France's S&P Global composite PMI showed business activity falling to a six-month low in November, with manufacturing weaker than services; the private sector is the most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012 (excluding early pandemic months), and job losses have been recorded for seven straight months.

Technical recession risk rose: a 0.1% Q3 GDP contraction is on record, and a further negative Q4 print would mean two consecutive negative quarters. The Bank of France's current Q4 projection is 0.4% growth, which its governor said 'might be a little bit too high', while maintaining that a recession is not forecast.

Pressure factors cited include a sharp rise in government borrowing costs (10-year yield near 5% in October per Nexity), Fitch's surprise outlook downgrade, weak domestic demand, election uncertainty ahead of April 2027, and large protests in October–November.

Goldman Sachs' Sharon Bell said a key factor is whether the recent spike in European energy prices eases; persistently high energy prices would mean higher inflation and rates, a particular problem for France as a vulnerable sovereign.
importance_reason: Signals rising technical-recession risk in the eurozone's second-largest economy, with sovereign-spread and election-related effects on corporate funding.
market_link: Higher French OAT yields and widening spread versus Bunds, pressure on French equities relative to European peers, and sensitivity to European energy prices and ECB rate expectations.

region: United Kingdom (England, with notes on Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland)
key_facts: The Renters' Rights Act, in force since May (this year), banned Section 21 'no-fault' evictions and made it illegal to refuse renting to families with children.

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies; per Savills (2024), around 40% of rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions versus 3% in the UK.

Savills expects 2026 to be another record year for institutional investment in build-to-rent (BTR); BTR homes tripled between 2019 and 2025 but still make up about 3% of the overall UK rental market. Grainger's CEO Helen Gordon believes BTR could reach 'at least 10%' over the next ten years.
Small landlords cite the Renters' Rights Act, rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including in the most recent Budget) as squeezing them; some are selling up.
importance_reason: Structural shift in UK rental market with policy and institutional-investment implications, but no single decisive market-moving event.
market_link: Growing institutional investment in build-to-rent could affect UK property/REIT and pension-fund allocations and rental-sector valuations; the effect is structural and gradual, not immediate.

key_facts: BBC investigation found a Whitby breeder (Mikjulora Dobermanns, Michael Estill) sold sick puppies, including Ozzy sold for £2,000 to Katie Thornton, who later incurred more than £5,000 in vet bills; the breeder had been downgraded from five-star to one-star rating two months before, but continued to advertise five-star.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council (August and December 2025) cited poor living conditions 'akin to a prison', deteriorating dog welfare, puppies not matching descriptions, and called the business 'more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder'; council renewed the licence in January 2026 but downgraded the rating to one-star.

BBC found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies with star ratings higher than their actual rating; a Facebook group of buyers mentioned 17 dogs that died before age eight, 10 of them below age four.
The council said the threshold for revoking the licence 'was not considered to have been met on the evidence available'; the breeder did not respond to BBC's request for comment.
importance_reason: Consumer-protection and regulatory investigation with no direct market impact; relevant only as a case study of weak licensing oversight.
